evidence.claim: Kishida was Japan's prime minister in 2022, a House of Representatives member, and the Hiroshima 1st District representative; the profile also records his prior foreign and defense posts.
evidence.title: KISHIDA Fumio (The Cabinet)
evidence.excerpt: Kishida was Japan's prime minister in 2022, a House of Representatives member, and the Hiroshima 1st District representative; the profile also records his prior foreign and defense posts.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary government biography maintained by the PMO; direct office and role evidence.
evidence.period_fit: Directly establishes ruler office and political identity during 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly Kishida's official profile; not inferred.

evidence.claim: Kishida made wage growth, larger public and private investment in people, skills and re-education, and a sustainable social security system oriented to all generations central to his 2022 policy agenda.
evidence.title: Policy Speech by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio to the 208th Session of the Diet
evidence.excerpt: Kishida made wage growth, larger public and private investment in people, skills and re-education, and a sustainable social security system oriented to all generations central to his 2022 policy agenda.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary, dated prime-ministerial policy speech from the target period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida statement as prime minister; strong attribution to ruler intent and policy direction.
contrary_evidence: This is an announced agenda, not proof of full implementation in 2022.

evidence.claim: Kishida said financial independence was the key to addressing women’s structural disadvantages and linked his cabinet’s agenda to correcting wage gaps and letting women work as they choose.
evidence.title: Video Message by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio on the Occasion of International Women’s Day
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said financial independence was the key to addressing women’s structural disadvantages and linked his cabinet’s agenda to correcting wage gaps and letting women work as they choose.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary, dated prime-ministerial statement with direct policy language.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida statement; strong attribution to ruler intent on gender and opportunity policy.
contrary_evidence: The message is rhetorical unless paired with later implementation evidence.

evidence.claim: The ministry added gender pay-gap disclosure to required reporting and made it mandatory for companies with 301 or more employees.
evidence.title: MHLW revised the Ordinance and Notification under the Women’s Active Engagement Promotion Act
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, Japan
evidence.excerpt: The ministry added gender pay-gap disclosure to required reporting and made it mandatory for companies with 301 or more employees.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary ministry rule-change notice with a specific effective date and enforceable obligation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Cabinet-era regulatory action tied in the notice to the new-capitalism execution plan; attribution is to Kishida administration rather than personal drafting.
contrary_evidence: The page shows rule design, not whether firms improved equality immediately.

evidence.claim: From October 1, 2022, both parents could divide childcare leave into two separate periods, expanding practical access to leave and care work sharing.
evidence.title: 育児休業 (Childcare leave)
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, Japan
evidence.excerpt: From October 1, 2022, both parents could divide childcare leave into two separate periods, expanding practical access to leave and care work sharing.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary ministry rule summary with the 2022 effective date stated plainly.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Cabinet-era labor policy implementation; attribution is to Kishida government policy environment, not a personal administrative act.
contrary_evidence: The page is a standing制度 page, so it does not show uptake or distributional effects.

evidence.claim: Kishida announced a new assistance system compensating 70 percent of fertilizer cost increases and said the money would be delivered quickly using reserve funds.
evidence.title: Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida
evidence.excerpt: Kishida announced a new assistance system compensating 70 percent of fertilizer cost increases and said the money would be delivered quickly using reserve funds.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary, dated prime-ministerial announcement with a precise policy amount and timing.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida announcement as prime minister; strong attribution to crisis-response policy choice.
contrary_evidence: This is a sectoral support measure, not proof of broad household welfare gains.

evidence.claim: The 2022 revised Child Welfare Act package strengthened child and family support, including municipal child-family center development and more integrated local support for children and families in difficulty.
evidence.title: 令和4年６月に成立した改正児童福祉法について
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, Japan
evidence.excerpt: The 2022 revised Child Welfare Act package strengthened child and family support, including municipal child-family center development and more integrated local support for children and families in difficulty.
evidence.source_locator: page summary section, lines 266-286 and linked June 2022 reform materials
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary ministry reform page; publication month is clear, but the page itself is a hub and not a single law text excerpt.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Cabinet-era social-policy reform under Kishida; attribution is to the administration and ministry system rather than sole personal authorship.
contrary_evidence: The hub page does not itself measure implementation or outcomes.

evidence.claim: The government said child-abuse consultation cases had continued to rise and abuse-related deaths had not ceased, and it adopted a new comprehensive countermeasure package including nationwide rollout of child-family centers and stronger child-consultation capacity.
evidence.title: 児童虐待防止対策の更なる推進について
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, Japan
evidence.excerpt: The government said child-abuse consultation cases had continued to rise and abuse-related deaths had not ceased, and it adopted a new comprehensive countermeasure package including nationwide rollout of child-family centers and stronger child-consultation capacity.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary ministry press release with a clear date and explicit policy response to worsening harm.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Cabinet and ministry action under Kishida; strong attribution to policy response, though the underlying abuse problem predates him.
contrary_evidence: The page acknowledges worsening abuse indicators, so it is partly a response to failure rather than a clean success story.

evidence.claim: Kishida said a diverse society, a social security system for all generations, stronger child-rearing support, active participation by women, loneliness and isolation measures, and urgent nursery-bus safety steps were part of his 2022 agenda.
evidence.title: Policy Speech by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio to the 210th Session of the Diet
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said a diverse society, a social security system for all generations, stronger child-rearing support, active participation by women, loneliness and isolation measures, and urgent nursery-bus safety steps were part of his 2022 agenda.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary, dated prime-ministerial speech with direct policy commitments.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida policy speech; strong attribution to ruler intent and agenda-setting.
contrary_evidence: The speech is agenda-setting and does not alone show downstream results.

evidence.claim: Kishida said the government would provide average households 47,000 yen in energy and LNG assistance, continue 100,000 yen in child-raising support without income caps, raise the childbirth lump-sum allowance to 500,000 yen, and move ahead with the Children and Families Agency.
evidence.title: Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said the government would provide average households 47,000 yen in energy and LNG assistance, continue 100,000 yen in child-raising support without income caps, raise the childbirth lump-sum allowance to 500,000 yen, and move ahead with the Children and Families Agency.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary, dated prime-ministerial press conference with specific amounts and institutional steps.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida announcement as prime minister; strong attribution to the administration’s crisis and family policy choices.
contrary_evidence: The relief is broad but temporary, and the page does not show whether it reversed 2022 real-income losses.

evidence.claim: For worker households in 2022, monthly income rose 2.0 percent nominally but fell 1.0 percent in real terms, while real consumption also lagged inflation.
evidence.title: 2022 Yearly Average Survey Results, Family Income and Expenditure Survey
evidence.excerpt: For worker households in 2022, monthly income rose 2.0 percent nominally but fell 1.0 percent in real terms, while real consumption also lagged inflation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary national statistics release, directly measuring household purchasing power for the target year.
evidence.period_fit: Target-year outcome released immediately after the window
evidence.ruler_attribution: Outcome context only; not uniquely attributable to Kishida, but it conditions the 2022 welfare assessment.
contrary_evidence: Nominal income rose even as real income fell, so the picture is mixed rather than uniformly negative.

evidence.claim: Japan’s child-related indicators show 98 percent measles vaccination, 99 percent DTP3 vaccination, 99 to 100 percent basic water and sanitation coverage, and 85 percent child social-protection coverage (latest listed as 2018 for that indicator).
evidence.title: Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Japan
evidence.excerpt: Japan’s child-related indicators show 98 percent measles vaccination, 99 percent DTP3 vaccination, 99 to 100 percent basic water and sanitation coverage, and 85 percent child social-protection coverage (latest listed as 2018 for that indicator).
evidence.source_locator: country dashboard indicators, especially lines 4943 and 5049-5064
evidence.source_confidence_reason: UNICEF data dashboard with clearly reported indicator values, though the page is a data hub and not a Kishida policy document.
evidence.period_fit: Country-level baseline context overlapping the target period
evidence.ruler_attribution: Baseline context only; these are inherited system indicators rather than evidence of Kishida-specific delivery in 2022.
contrary_evidence: The child-social-protection figure is dated 2018, so it is not a 2022 ruler outcome.

evidence.claim: The OECD said Japan’s pandemic-era adult-learning response focused on improving career guidance, broadening training participation, and fostering teleworking, while also addressing inequalities in skills and training across socio-demographic groups.
evidence.title: The New Workplace in Japan: Skills for a Strong Recovery
evidence.excerpt: The OECD said Japan’s pandemic-era adult-learning response focused on improving career guidance, broadening training participation, and fostering teleworking, while also addressing inequalities in skills and training across socio-demographic groups.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary OECD country report, closely timed to the target year and specific about policy efforts and constraints.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly system-level context; it overlaps with Kishida’s human-investment agenda but is not itself a Kishida decision record.
contrary_evidence: The report is analytical context, not proof of Kishida’s direct authorship or 2022 implementation success.

evidence.claim: The OECD described Japan as having the longest life expectancy in the OECD and very strong prevention systems, while noting the challenge of rapid population ageing and chronic disease.
evidence.title: OECD Reviews of Public Health: Japan
evidence.excerpt: The OECD described Japan as having the longest life expectancy in the OECD and very strong prevention systems, while noting the challenge of rapid population ageing and chronic disease.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary OECD review with a precise country assessment and clear structural constraints.
evidence.period_fit: Inherited baseline and constraint context for 2022
evidence.ruler_attribution: Context only; it supports the inherited baseline rather than Kishida-specific causation.
contrary_evidence: A strong inherited public-health system limits how much credit can be assigned to a single 2022 administration.

unresolved_gaps: Direct cabinet-level records on Kishida's private command-and-control choices around safeguards, emergency procedures, and technical nuclear governance are thin.
Direct evidence of behind-the-scenes mediation, ceasefire brokerage, or proxy-control choices is thin.
The dossier remains thin on a ruler-specific pre-July 2022 domestic protection record, so most of the strong evidence is reactive to the Abe assassination and the Unification Church fallout.
Direct evidence of court, media, or election-administration capture attempts by Kishida is thin; most negative evidence is baseline openness plus remedial scandal cleanup.
Direct anti-capture, procurement, or favoritism evidence is thin relative to the amount of policy and macroeconomic material.
Subgroup-specific uptake and outcome evidence for poverty, disability, migrants, and regional disparities remains thin.
The dossier lacks direct 2022 evidence on Kishida's own assets, gifts, campaign finance, hidden conflicts, or family enrichment.
Independent evaluation of New Capitalism implementation and the causal contribution of Kishida's team remains limited; several follow-up items are government self-assessments or macro context.
